title: Vortex
summary: Self-hosted media streaming across three runtimes — Android phones & tablets, Android TV and Windows — one Kotlin codebase, one library from your own Google Drive, SMB, SFTP, FTP, WebDAV, NFS and UPnP sources, plus a YouTube-powered music library.
description: Vortex is a client-side, self-hosted media streaming application with no backend and no subscription: it streams directly from sources you already own. A single Kotlin codebase ships three runtimes — Android phones and tablets, Android TV, and a Compose Multiplatform desktop app for Windows. It aggregates personal media libraries from Google Drive, SMB, SFTP, FTP/FTPS, WebDAV, NFS and UPnP into one unified library, enriches everything with TMDB metadata, and plays movies and TV with Media3/ExoPlayer on mobile and TV or an in-app mpv player on the desktop. On top of movies and TV it adds a YouTube-powered music library with real offline downloads, user profiles, custom collections, actor pages and more.

runtimes.label: Android
runtimes.description: Phones and tablets — touch UI with metadata, resume, downloads, profiles, music and offline support.

runtimes.label: TV
runtimes.description: Android TV — Leanback launcher, D-pad navigation, remote controls and an ambient poster-slideshow screensaver.

runtimes.label: PC
runtimes.description: Windows desktop — Netflix-style library in Compose Multiplatform, in-app mpv player with external fallback, Drive sign-in via OAuth loopback and real 4K / HDR / Dolby Vision / Atmos quality badges.

features: Unified movie & TV library aggregated from Google Drive, SMB, SFTP, FTP/FTPS, WebDAV, NFS and UPnP
TMDB metadata enrichment — posters, backdrops, cast, episode details — with manual re-matching
Per-title and per-episode playback resume, scoped per profile
Subtitle track selection, styling, offset and per-show language memory; sidecar subtitle scanning
Multi-track audio selection and playback speeds (0.5× – 2.0×)
Google Drive OAuth — embedded WebView flow on TV (device-flow fallback), Google Sign-In on phone, browser loopback on desktop
Offline downloads for every provider via a WorkManager queue with pause, resume, retry and progress
Download controls — storage location picker, Wi-Fi-only mode, free-space guard, quota-based auto cleanup
Android TV: Leanback launcher, D-pad navigation and an ambient poster-slideshow screensaver
LAN server discovery (NSD/mDNS) that pre-fills connection forms for SMB/SFTP/FTP/WebDAV
User profiles with per-profile favorites, watchlist, watched, resume and subtitle memory; kids profiles
Custom collections and watchlists with ordered membership
Music: on-device YouTube search, streaming playback, real offline audio downloads, playlists with M3U import/export
Actor & director pages and "You May Also Like" similar titles from clickable cast
Per-episode watched state (auto at 95%+) with season progress bars
Playback diagnostics overlay — codecs, resolution, dropped frames, bandwidth estimate
Backup & restore as versioned JSON (merge-only, secrets never exported)
Equalizer, audio routing and ambient display while playing
RAM-only stream buffering — no stream bytes ever written to disk
Desktop (Windows): in-app mpv player (mediamp) with external-mpv fallback, real 4K / HDR / Dolby Vision / Atmos quality probing and yt-dlp trailers
partialFeatures: YouTube as a video media source via the NewPipe extractor — present in code, experimental, not a headline flow
Music screens are phone-only — TV music/equalizer is a documented follow-up
architecture: A single Kotlin codebase with no backend. A remote-storage provider layer abstracts Google Drive, SMB, SFTP, FTP, WebDAV, NFS and UPnP behind one interface, with LAN discovery (NSD/mDNS) to pre-fill connections; a repository layer feeds a Room database that drives the Compose UI on phones, TV and — via a shared Kotlin Multiplatform core — the Compose Multiplatform desktop app. TMDB metadata is fetched and cached locally (24 h TTL). Playback is Media3/ExoPlayer on mobile and TV, and an in-app mpv player (mediamp) on desktop, where a loopback DriveStreamProxy injects OAuth credentials so mpv can stream authenticated Drive URLs. Secrets (connection passwords, SSH keys, OAuth tokens) live in an Android Keystore-backed encrypted store — never in Room.
architectureDiagram:
Presentation — Compose (phone) · Compose TV (TV) · Compose Multiplatform (desktop)
        ↓  shared Kotlin Multiplatform core
Repository layer — Room DB · per-profile state · TMDB cache
        ↓
Remote storage providers
Drive · SMB · SFTP · FTP · WebDAV · UPnP · NFS  (+ LAN discovery)
        ↓
Playback
Media3 / ExoPlayer (mobile · TV)  ·  mpv / mediamp (desktop)
Secrets — Android Keystore (never Room) · desktop loopback DriveStreamProxy
limitations: Requires TMDB and Google OAuth credentials in local.properties — the app cannot build without them
Google TV OAuth client secrets live in gitignored files (TV SECRET.json / WEB Secret.json) and must not be committed
No iOS build — Kotlin/Compose only
Backup & restore is gated off on Android TV (no DocumentsUI/SAF pickers)
Optional cross-device sync and the provider/add-on architecture are still pending design decisions
futureWork: Cross-device sync — documented plan that needs a self-hosted service decision (auth, encryption, conflict resolution)
Provider / add-on architecture — manifest format and resolver isolation design pending
Release readiness: final signed release build and Play Console submission
On-device QA pass across the phone / tablet / TV device matrix

title: Cheltuieli
summary: A PyQt6 desktop expense tracker that scans IMAP inboxes for invoices, extracts amounts with OCR and PDF parsing, and exports everything to formatted Excel.
description: Cheltuieli automates the boring part of expense tracking: it connects to an IMAP mailbox (presets for Gmail, Outlook, Yahoo and iCloud), scans messages and attachments, extracts invoice text from HTML, PDFs and images via Tesseract OCR, matches amounts with configurable keywords, and writes a formatted Excel workbook with automatic backups. Scanning runs in background threads so the UI stays responsive.
features: IMAP mailbox scanning with provider presets (Gmail, Outlook/Hotmail, Yahoo, iCloud)
Attachment extraction from HTML, PDF and image formats
Invoice text extraction with configurable sender/subject/keyword filters
OCR via Tesseract with a configurable tesseract path
Excel export with formatting and automatic backups to backup/
Async scan workers (QThread) so the UI never freezes
Settings persisted to settings.json with defaults
Windows build via build.bat (venv + PyInstaller)
architecture: PyQt6 UI drives background QThread workers. EmailScanner handles IMAP connections and mailbox listing; InvoiceExtractor decodes messages and extracts text from HTML/PDF/image attachments (Tesseract for images); ExcelHandler writes the formatted workbook. SettingsManager keeps configuration and provider presets in settings.json.
architectureDiagram:
PyQt6 UI (main_window)
    ↓  QThread workers
EmailScanner (IMAP)
    ↓
InvoiceExtractor (HTML · PDF · OCR)
    ↓
ExcelHandler (openpyxl + backups)
limitations: Requires a local Tesseract installation for image OCR
Matching depends on keyword configuration — accuracy varies by supplier

title: Auto Oferta · Teka
summary: Offline offer generator for Teka: reads six Excel files (products, clients, promos), applies tiered discounts, and exports client offers — as a Windows app and an Android app.
description: Auto Oferta is a local tool built for Teka that centralizes six Excel workbooks (sinks, kitchen taps, appliances, accessories, client commercial conditions, brochures/promos). It matches clients with products, applies commercial discounts, calculates final prices with configurable TVA and promo formulas, and exports the result to Excel. A local Python server serves an offline web interface, wrapped for Android via Capacitor, with a single-file Windows build via PyInstaller.
features: Loads six Excel sources with sheet/header detection and column aliasing (incl. legacy .xls)
Client-to-product matching across commercial conditions
Tiered discount engine — client discount then supplementary discount, applied cascaded (not summed)
Promo modes: brochure 'ADAOS 20%' and percentage discounts
Configurable TVA (default 21%) and promo formulas
Excel export of calculated offers
Mock data generator for local testing
Portable single-file Windows build (PyInstaller) with settings next to the exe
Android wrapper via Capacitor
Unit tests (unittest discover -s tests)
architecture: excel_loader.py normalizes the six workbooks, service.py performs client/product/promo matching, pricing.py owns the tiered-discount formulas, exporter.py writes results, and app.py serves the offline web dashboard on localhost. The Capacitor project wraps the same web UI for Android.
architectureDiagram:
6 Excel workbooks
    ↓  excel_loader (aliases, normalization)
service.py (matching)
    ↓
pricing.py (tiered discounts · TVA · promos)
    ↓
exporter.py → Excel offer  ·  app.py → local web UI → Capacitor (Android)
limitations: Pricing formulas are specific to Teka's commercial conditions — not generic
Local-first: no multi-user or server deployment

title: Apps Manager
summary: An Electron launcher that scans drives for games and apps, installs software through winget, and tracks playtime — all in one SQLite-backed dashboard.
description: Apps Manager is an Electron desktop app that turns a machine into a tidy launcher. It scans configured paths to detect installed games, lets you add or rename entries and set custom covers, launches games while recording playtime, and installs applications through winget with a progress UI. Everything is stored locally in SQLite (better-sqlite3).
features: Game detection by scanning configured paths
Manual add/remove/rename of entries with custom covers
Launch games with last-played and playtime tracking
winget-based app installation with progress feedback
Floating scan overlay and install progress bar
SQLite library (games + winget databases) with seed data
Settings persisted in the Electron userData directory
architecture: The Electron main process owns SQLite (better-sqlite3) and exposes a typed API over contextBridge via preload. The React renderer (Vite) consumes it through tabs — DetectGames, InstallApps, StartApp, Settings — with a floating overlay for background scans.
architectureDiagram:
React UI (Vite renderer)
    ↑  contextBridge API
Electron main process
    ├─ better-sqlite3 (games, winget)
    └─ winget CLI integration
limitations: Early-stage — README is still the create-vite template
Windows-specific (winget, exe paths)

title: Dataset Generator
summary: A desktop tool for building image datasets from multiple sources — Bing, Google, iCrawler — and generating SAM-based masks and annotation files for training.
description: Dataset Generator assembles image datasets from several scraping backends with user-agent spoofing and organized temp management, then supports mask generation with Segment Anything and annotation classes defined in JSON. Two CustomTkinter front-ends (app/ and new_ui/) drive the pipeline, and it ships with the CUDA-toolchain requirements for on-machine training.
features: Multi-source image download (Bing, Google Images, iCrawler) with fake-user-agent spoofing
Organized download into per-class folders with temp-directory management
SAM-based mask generation for annotation
Annotation class definitions in annotation_classes.json
Two GUI generations (app/ and new_ui/) plus CLI entry points
run.ps1 launcher scripts for Windows
architecture: MultiSourceDatasetGenerator orchestrates the scraping backends and file organization; mask_generator.py wraps Segment Anything for mask outputs; the CustomTkinter GUIs bind these into a desktop flow. Requirements pin the PyTorch CUDA 12.4 toolchain.
architectureDiagram:
CustomTkinter GUI
    ↓
MultiSourceDatasetGenerator (Bing · Google · iCrawler)
    ↓
organized dataset → mask_generator (SAM) → annotations
limitations: Scraping reliability depends on the upstream image services
SAM mask generation requires the SAM weights and a GPU for practical use

title: Detectie
summary: An end-to-end license-plate detection system: YOLO + OCR on a Python WebSocket server, an ESP32 firmware client, and a phone-camera capture page.
description: Detectie is a complete detection pipeline: a desktop app (PySide6) trains and tests YOLO models for plates, a Python server runs YOLO detection plus EasyOCR recognition and exposes a WebSocket API, an ESP32 client (PlatformIO/Arduino) receives results in real time, and a phone-camera HTML page feeds captures from a browser. It was built as a project with its own documentation (DOCUMENTATIE_PROIECT.md).
features: YOLO-based license-plate detection with confidence filtering
OCR of the cropped plate region with EasyOCR
WebSocket server streaming detection results
ESP32 firmware: Wi-Fi with auto-reconnect, JSON messages, role registration
Phone-camera capture page for sending images from a browser
PySide6 training app with train/finetune/test tabs (shared with YOLO-Trainer)
Project documentation in DOCUMENTATIE_PROIECT.md
architecture: server.py runs YOLO inference and EasyOCR over async WebSockets and returns PlateResult objects (index, confidence, bbox, recognized text, crop path). The ESP32 connects as a client and renders results; phone_camera_client.html captures and uploads images. Models are trained offline with the PySide6 Train_APP.
architectureDiagram:
Phone camera / camera feed
    ↓
Python server (YOLO → EasyOCR) ── WebSocket API
    ↓
ESP32 client (PlatformIO)  ·  web results

PySide6 Train_APP trains the YOLO weights offline
limitations: Wi-Fi SSID, password and server IP are hardcoded in the ESP32 firmware — should move to build-time config
Tied to a local network (single server address)
Detection quality depends on the trained plate model
futureWork: Move network credentials out of src/main.cpp into PlatformIO build flags

title: OmniStudio
summary: A local workspace for running LLMs: scan GGUF models, manage llama.cpp servers, chat with persistent conversations, and watch GPU stats — as a Tauri desktop app with a React UI.
description: OmniStudio is a local AI runtime manager. The Tauri desktop app (Rust core, React UI) scans and registers llama.cpp backends, parses GGUF metadata (architecture, quantization, context length, tokenizer), stores model folders and conversations, streams chat tokens, and polls hardware stats via sysinfo. A companion web build pairs a Vite/React frontend with a FastAPI backend that launches llama-server subprocesses with configurable context, GPU layers and threads, streams chat completions with built-in tools, and polls system/GPU stats. The Image and Video Studio tabs are currently placeholders that return generated preview SVGs — the real generation pipeline is not built yet.
features: Backend registry: scan for llama.cpp executables, add custom backends, remove, poll state
Model management: add model folders, rescan, parse GGUF metadata
GGUF model scanning and profile management (settings persisted to JSON)
llama-server process manager — context size, GPU layers, threads, batch, cache type
Chat with streaming completions and tool-calling (calculator, web search, file parser)
Chat with streaming tokens and persistent conversations
Hugging Face model download UI
Live system stats and GPU VRAM polling
Hardware statistics polling (CPU/GPU via sysinfo) with subscribers
Backend capability inspection and refresh (dynamic loading)
Native file and folder browsing
Settings and UI state persisted via zustand stores
Windows/DXGI integration in the Rust core
Mock llama-server for testing the UI without a model
partialFeatures: Image Studio / Video Studio — endpoints exist but return placeholder SVGs / sample video, not real generation
architecture: The Rust core (tauri commands + sysinfo + libloading) owns hardware, model metadata and backend lifecycle; React services wrap Tauri invoke() calls and poll state. The web build runs a FastAPI backend whose LlamaProcessManager spawns llama-server as a subprocess with a model config and tracks status, PID, uptime and a log ring buffer — the React app polls status and stats and talks to models over the OpenAI-compatible API. Tool execution runs in the backend tool runner; zustand stores keep settings and UI state.
architectureDiagram:
React UI (Tauri desktop · web)
    ↑  Tauri commands / HTTP + polling
Rust core (sysinfo · GGUF parser · libloading) / FastAPI backend
    ├─ backend registry → llama-server / llama.cpp
    ├─ config_manager → profiles/settings (JSON)
    └─ tool_runner → calculator / web_search / file_parser
limitations: Early stage (v0.1.0, 3 commits) — chat depends on a backend being registered
Image and video generation are mocked — no real diffusion pipeline yet
Requires llama.cpp binaries and GGUF models to be present locally
Rust core requires a Tauri build toolchain

title: Primarie (E-Services Portal)
summary: A municipal e-services portal — declarations, tax certificates and fine payments in one account — with scrypt auth, role-based dashboards, audit logging and SQLite storage.
description: Primarie is a Next.js portal for municipal e-services. It ships with a seeded demo user, scrypt password hashing with an optional pepper, brute-force throttling on login, a guided declaration wizard, role-based dashboard views (an OWASP A01 access-control pass is recorded in git history), audit logging, and a performance pass that lifted its audit score to 84/100. Data lives in SQLite (node:sqlite) with a JSON store for legacy content, and the whole thing deploys via a multi-stage Dockerfile. A fully interactive static demo (client-side state in localStorage) is published on GitHub Pages.
features: Authentication with scrypt hashing, pepper support and login throttling (5 attempts / 15 min)
Seeded demo user for evaluation
Guided declaration wizard
Role-based dashboard views with access control
Audit logging of sensitive actions
SQLite system of record (users, sessions) plus JSON store for declarations/certificates/payments
Fine search and online payment (plata amenzi)
Certificate verification by code
Contact, legislation and FAQ pages
Multi-stage Docker deployment as non-root user
Documented performance audits (84/100 on second pass)
Static GitHub Pages demo with client-side persisted state
architecture: Server actions validate input (validate.ts), manage sessions and audit (audit.ts, auth.ts). Declarations flow through lib/declarations.ts and forms.ts against SQLite, with a JSON database for content that predates the migration. The Dockerfile builds a standalone Next.js output. In the Pages demo build, lib/auth.ts and lib/db.ts serve a seeded client-side store instead, so the whole dashboard stays interactive without a server.
architectureDiagram:
Browser
    ↓  Server Actions
Next.js (App Router)
    ├─ auth.ts (scrypt · pepper · throttle)
    ├─ declarations.ts / forms.ts
    ├─ SQLite (node:sqlite) + data/db.json
    └─ audit.ts → data/logs

GitHub Pages demo: seeded client store (localStorage)
limitations: Demo credentials are hardcoded in lib/auth.ts — fine for evaluation, must be replaced for production
JSON store is being migrated to SQLite; both are read at runtime

title: Coral Tech · FTC team site
summary: Bilingual (EN/RO) website for an FTC robotics team with a local-LLM RAG chatbot that answers from the site's own content, citing sources.
description: Coral Tech is the website of an FTC robotics team (#28260) — "fusing nature with technology". It's bilingual (English/Romanian), covers seasons, activities, sponsors, the team and a blog, and includes a RAG chatbot: content is embedded with local Ollama models into a persisted vector store, and the chat endpoint retrieves chunks, answers with a local GGUF model (node-llama-cpp), and returns structured actions (scroll to a section) plus sources. Admin auth uses WebAuthn passkeys.
features: Bilingual content (EN/RO) with locale files
Content model: activities, seasons, sponsors, team, blog posts
RAG chat over local vectors with structured answers, action buttons and cited sources
Content sync + reindex endpoint with fingerprint caching
File-watcher triggered background refresh on content changes
Admin authentication with WebAuthn passkeys
Local GGUF model configuration (model path, temperature, max tokens, context)
architecture: The RAG pipeline embeds site content with Ollama, stores vectors in data/rag/vectors.json, and loads them in memory for cosine/hybrid retrieval. Chat answers are generated by a local GGUF model via node-llama-cpp, with the response schema returning answer, actions, sources and language. A sync endpoint rebuilds the website snapshot and can reindex vectors.
architectureDiagram:
Site content (content/ · app/ · locales/)
    ↓  sync + embed (Ollama)
Vector store (data/rag/vectors.json)
    ↓  retrieve
/api/rag/chat → local GGUF (node-llama-cpp) → answer + sources + actions
limitations: Chat requires Ollama and the GGUF model to be running locally
Vector store is file-based JSON — fine for a small site

title: Liceul Teoretic Ion Cantacuzino
summary: A complete school website — news, classes, teachers directory, documents, gallery, e-learning and timetable — with a SQLite-backed admin panel.
description: A production-style website for Liceul Teoretic Ion Cantacuzino built on Next.js. It publishes news, classes, teachers, documents, results, gallery and a school magazine, plus e-learning and timetable pages. Content is managed through an admin panel (JWT sessions, bcrypt-hashed passwords) and stored in SQLite (better-sqlite3), migrated from a legacy JSON data store by a one-time migration script that refuses to run over existing data.
features: Content entities: settings, news, classes, teachers, gallery, documents, results, pages
Admin panel with JWT sessions and bcrypt password hashing
SQLite storage with JSON → SQLite one-time migration (guarded by a migration key)
Public pages: news, classes, teachers directory, documents, gallery, magazine, e-learning, timetable
Server-rendered pages with loading/error boundaries
Theme toggle and animated reveals (framer-motion)
architecture: lib/db.ts wraps better-sqlite3; content-store.ts provides the content layer over all entities. Server actions and API routes read/write SQLite, and the admin flow issues signed JWTs. The migration script (scripts/migrate-json-to-sqlite.ts) imports legacy JSON only when the database is empty and unmarked.
architectureDiagram:
Public pages (news · classes · teachers · gallery …)
    ↑  content-store.ts
SQLite (data/db.sqlite)
    ↑  admin panel (JWT + bcrypt) · migration guard

title: YOLO Trainer
summary: A PySide6 desktop app for training, fine-tuning and testing YOLO models (v8/11/26) with live logs, metric charts, GPU checks and a packaged Windows installer.
description: YOLO Trainer is a desktop GUI around Ultralytics training. It splits the workflow into Train, Fine-tune and Test tabs, runs training in a QThread so the UI stays live, plots metrics with pyqtgraph, validates datasets and presets, and supports inference on images, videos or folders. It can be packaged as a Windows installer (PyInstaller + Inno Setup) and supports WebSocket-based remote inference.
features: Train / fine-tune / test tabs with preset configurations
Background training via QThread with live logs and progress
Metric plotting (pyqtgraph / matplotlib)
Inference testing on images, video and folders
Dataset validation before training
GPU detection and configuration
Dark theme UI
Windows installer packaging (PyInstaller spec + Inno Setup script)
WebSocket-based remote inference
architecture: Training runs in a QThread worker (workers/training_worker.py) that reports logs and metrics to the UI; services wrap Ultralytics, GPU discovery, dataset validation and preset loading; widgets render logs and metric plots; inference workers handle test-time detection.
architectureDiagram:
PySide6 UI (tabs: train · finetune · test)
    ↓  QThread workers
Ultralytics YOLO (train / finetune / predict)
    ├─ dataset_service (validation)
    ├─ gpu_service (CUDA)
    └─ preset_service (YAML presets)
limitations: Training requires the PyTorch/CUDA toolchain
WebSocket inference needs a running receiver

title: Jarvis · OS Helper
summary: A local-first AI operating assistant: a 9B planner, a 26M executor, 56 tools, and an offline keyword router so everything keeps working without a model server.
description: Jarvis is a local-first, extensible AI assistant built on the @earendil-works/pi framework. It uses a three-layer architecture — Ornith (9B) plans but never calls tools, Needle (26M) picks tool + args but never chats, and the runtime validates, checks permissions, executes and logs. There are 56 tools across filesystem, shell, Windows, Excel, browser, memory, media, system, archive, document, image, AI, automation and dev groups. A correction layer routes intents offline — fixing typos, Unix aliases and known failure modes — so all tools stay reachable even when no model is running. The media manager syncs a Google Drive / local library and talks to qBittorrent and rclone.
features: Three-layer agent architecture: planner (9B) → executor (26M) → runtime
56 tools in 14 groups with a permissions system (safe/ask)
Offline correction-layer router: typo tolerance, Unix aliases, multilingual hints, legacy failure fixes
Media manager: filelist (SQLite-cached library), drive (rclone), torrent (qBittorrent WebUI)
Persistence: media index and memory stores in SQLite
GPU Docker workspace (CUDA Jupyter) via docker-compose
Test suite (Jest) covering executor, permissions, media and tools
Documentation for installation, extensions, workflows and model optimization
architecture: Queries flow User → Ornith (planner) → Needle (executor) → Runtime → Tools. The runtime validates and gates tool calls by permission; when Needle is unavailable, correction.ts routes intents via a prioritized keyword scorer so the same tools stay reachable offline. Media tooling caches library state in media_index.db and integrates rclone + qBittorrent.
architectureDiagram:
User
  ↓
Ornith (planner, 9B) — plans, never calls tools
  ↓
Needle (executor, 26M) — picks tool + args
  ↓
Runtime (validate · permissions · execute · log)
  ↓
56 tools — filesystem · shell · windows · excel · browser · media · AI …

correction.ts routes intents offline when Needle is down
limitations: Relies on the @earendil-works/pi framework as the host platform
Requires bundled binaries (ffmpeg, rclone) and optional qBittorrent for media tools

title: Siteauto
summary: A car-parts shop with AI detection: upload a photo and a custom YOLOv8 model identifies the part and matches products — plus cart, checkout, appointments and a dashboard.
description: Siteauto is a Next.js storefront for car parts with a computer-vision twist: the detect page accepts a photo, runs a custom-trained YOLOv8 model (there are variants trained with and without side mirrors), draws the detected part on a canvas and filters matching products. The store itself has products, a cart (Redis-backed), checkout, JWT auth, service appointments, a dashboard for cars and messages, 3D product models and a floating chat widget. The detection runs through a Python helper spawned by the Next.js API route.
features: Photo upload with canvas preview and YOLOv8 part detection (custom model, .15 confidence floor)
Detection results matched against store products
Shop with product pages and 3D product models
Cart + checkout flow
Register/login with JWT sessions
Service appointments and dashboard (appointments, cars, messages)
Floating chat widget
Docker deployment with Python/OpenCV system deps
architecture: app/api/detect/route.js spawns utils/detect.py (Ultralytics YOLO + OpenCV) as a child process, parses its JSON output, and matches classes to products. The store layer uses Redis via lib/redis.js for cart state, and JWT middleware guards the dashboard/checkout routes. Custom .pt models live in model/.
architectureDiagram:
Browser (upload photo)
    ↓
Next.js /api/detect → python utils/detect.py (YOLOv8)
    ↓  JSON detections
product matching → shop / cart (Redis) / checkout (JWT)
limitations: Requires Redis running locally for cart functionality
Detection runs a Python subprocess per request — fine for a demo, not for scale
Model files (.pt) are large binaries kept in the repo

title: AI Interface
summary: A small Flask app that classifies uploaded images with locally loaded TensorFlow models, plus a helper that indexes a folder into a dataset manifest.
description: AI Interface is a compact experiment: a Flask web app that loads Keras models registered in models.json, accepts an image upload, runs inference with the selected model and returns the predicted class. A companion tkinter script walks a directory of images and writes top_level_folders.json — a small helper for assembling image datasets for training.
features: Image upload and classification against a user-selected model
Model registry in models.json mapping keys to .h5 weights and label files
GET /models endpoint listing available models
Folder-indexing helper that writes top_level_folders.json from a directory
architecture: A single Flask process serves the HTML frontend from templates/, accepts uploads into uploads/, and runs tf.keras inference per request. Models are loaded from .h5 files on disk per the models.json registry.
limitations: One-shot inference only — no batching, no GPU path, no error fallback beyond the Flask defaults
Models must be placed manually under models/

title: LLM Finetuner
summary: A Flask web interface for fine-tuning LLMs with Unsloth — LoRA parameters, live GPU monitoring, custom chat templates and training resume.
description: LLM Finetuner puts Unsloth-based LoRA fine-tuning behind a web UI. It ships with model presets (Llama 3.2 1B, Mistral 7B 4-bit), configurable LoRA/training parameters, GPU/CPU/system metrics streamed from the backend, custom chat templates, live training logs and a resume flow. Heavy imports (Unsloth, TRL, Transformers) load lazily so the UI stays responsive, and everything runs locally.
features: Fine-tune any Unsloth-compatible model from a web form
Model presets in config/models.json (e.g. Llama 3.2 1B Instruct, Mistral 7B v0.3, 4-bit variants)
Configurable LoRA + training parameters (rank, alpha, dropout, batch, grad accumulation, warmup, max steps, learning rate)
Custom chat template support with defaults in config/default_template.json
Live GPU / CPU / system metrics (nvidia-smi, WMI/win32pdh on Windows, psutil)
Live training logs and status tracking
Training resume from a saved state (resume.html)
Lazy loading of heavy ML imports; uploads and cache directories managed by the app
Example training dataset included (data.json — car-diagnostics chat pairs)
architecture: Flask serves the web UI and defers to a lazily-imported finetunerLLM module that drives Unsloth's FastLanguageModel with TRL's SFTTrainer. Training runs on a background thread while a status object tracks progress and messages. Config lives in JSON files under config/ (models, default settings, templates).
architectureDiagram:
Browser (index · resume)
    ↓
Flask app.py

title: NeuroShell
summary: A Claude Code-style terminal AI shell: slash commands, tab completion, instant model hot-swapping across Ollama/GGUF/Transformers/HF/OpenAI, and a sandboxed tool loop.
description: NeuroShell is an interactive terminal shell and autonomous tool-using AI agent. It brings a Claude Code-like command interface with a slash-command palette, real-time tab autocompletion, instant model swapping across five backends (Ollama, local GGUF, PyTorch Transformers, Hugging Face cloud, OpenAI-compatible endpoints), and a sandboxed tool-execution loop that restricts filesystem and terminal actions to the configured workspace. It includes a GPU device abstraction (CUDA with automatic CPU fallback), Hugging Face model downloads with cache management, dialogue memory, RAG command indexing, and optional voice input/output.
features: Interactive REPL with a slash-command palette (/help, /model, /gpu, /download, /clear, /tools, /mode, /history, /exit)
Real-time tab autocompletion for commands, models, Hugging Face repos and workspace paths
Instant model hot-swapping across Ollama, local GGUF, Transformers, HF Cloud and OpenAI-compatible endpoints
Autonomous tool-use loop with planning, intent classification, task state and reflection modules
Sandboxed execution: filesystem/terminal restricted to the workspace; dangerous commands blocked; Safe Mode asks before modifying
GPU device abstraction with /gpu diagnostics (device, name, VRAM) and CPU fallback
Hugging Face model downloading with cache management (HF_HOME isolated)
Dialogue history (JSONL) and execution memory
RAG command indexing and project-aware helpers (project detection, brain, summarizer)
Optional voice: STT/TTS with wake word and auto language detection
PyInstaller-friendly entry point with pip-subprocess support
architecture: A prompt_toolkit REPL (ui/cli.py) drives a turn loop (core/loop.py) that routes intents through a tool router to sandboxed executors. Models are managed by models/manager.py across five providers, with a GPU device layer (gpu/device.py) mapping tensors to cuda:0 or cpu. State (config, registry, history) lives under ~/.neuroshell/, with caches isolated there too.

Terminal REPL (prompt_toolkit)
    ↓
core/loop (agent · planner · router)
    ↓
tools (terminal · filesystem · system · web) — sandboxed
    ↑
models/manager → ollama · GGUF · transformers · HF · OpenAI
limitations: Local model quality depends on the active backend/model
Requires Python 3.10+ and (for GPU) an NVIDIA GPU with the CUDA wheels

title: Handwritten PDF → Typed PDF
summary: A local desktop app that converts handwritten PDF pages — including math — into clean typed PDFs, powered by GLM-OCR via Ollama or Transformers.
description: This app turns scanned handwritten PDFs (including formulas) into clean typed PDFs entirely on your machine. A Tkinter GUI (the default mode) picks an input PDF, chooses a backend — an Ollama model like glm-ocr:q8_0, a custom GGUF imported into Ollama, or the zai-org/GLM-OCR Transformers model — and produces a typeset PDF via ReportLab with LaTeX-style math rendered through matplotlib mathtext. A FastAPI backend is also available for scripted use, with job tracking, per-page progress and timeouts.
features: Convert handwritten PDF pages (incl. math) to typed PDF locally
Two OCR backends: Ollama model tag (default glm-ocr:q8_0) or zai-org/GLM-OCR via Transformers
Custom GGUF import into Ollama on convert
Prompt modes for text, formula and table recognition
Math rendering with matplotlib mathtext in the output PDF
Unicode-safe PDF fonts (DejaVu) via ReportLab
Tkinter GUI with progress panel, page/pass progress and heartbeat updates
FastAPI API mode with job tracking, uploads and CORS for local frontends
Configurable DPI, max tokens, page timeout and runtime limits
Large pages resized automatically for reliability
architecture: FastAPI (v1.0) exposes conversion endpoints backed by ocr_service.py (backend selection, Ollama client, GLM-OCR Transformers path) and pdf_processing.py (page rendering with PyMuPDF, typed PDF assembly with ReportLab and matplotlib math). The Tkinter GUI drives the same pipeline. Jobs run with per-page timeouts and a shared inference lock.
architectureDiagram:

        ↓
ocr_service — ollama | transformers (GLM-OCR)
        ↓
pdf_processing — PyMuPDF → ReportLab (+ matplotlib math)
        ↓
typed PDF
limitations: Requires Ollama running locally for the Ollama backend, or the GLM-OCR Transformers model for the transformers backend
GPU recommended for speed (CPU works)
Recognition quality varies with handwriting and the chosen model
